title: 把 RNA folding 偷進 GHC——ApplicativeDo 排程的 Nussinov DP 重寫
summary: Ian Duncan 重新啟用 GHC 一個長期被 -foptimal-applicative-do flag 隱藏的優化：把 do-block 排程對應到 RNA 二級結構摺疊，套用 Nussinov 1978 的區間動態規劃並加上 longest-chain bound 剪枝。1,000-statement worst case 從 55 秒降到秒級。
widget_questions: Which stage of GHC's ApplicativeDo desugaring pipeline is the structural analogue of each RNA-folding concept (base ↔ statement, complementary bond ↔ dependency edge, optimal fold ↔ minimal-round-trip schedule)?
How fast does the naive cut-check cost explode as the do-block grows from 10 to 1,000 statements, and where does the optimised algorithm (longest-chain bound) pull the curve back?
Across realistic versus adversarial do-block inputs, how much of the search space does the longest-chain bound prune — and why does the improvement ratio behave differently in the two regimes?
How does a single recurrence describe both an RNA hairpin and a Haskell ApplicativeDo schedule simultaneously, and what changes between the two interpretations?
What are the three Nussinov DP transitions (drop i, pair (i, j), split at k), and how does each map to a Haskell scheduling decision?
At a single DP cell, how does the longest-chain lower bound interact with the running 'best' value to short-circuit the remaining split-point scan?
When you flip the input distribution from adversarial chain to realistic mix, why does the improvement ratio collapse from 67× to 3.2× even though the absolute prune savings remain meaningful?
Which target languages and scheduler domains can directly absorb Nussinov-style interval DP, and which already have a more mature toolbox or a structurally incompatible search space?
What ancillary affordance hints (sort, switch, toggle) does the post offer the reader to discover its interactive widgets without scanning prose?
